title: Rome
subtitle: The rise and fall of an empire, 753 BC to 1453

steps.title: A city on the Tiber
steps.text: Roman tradition dated the founding of the city to 753 BC. In the legend the twins Romulus and Remus, sons of Mars, were raised by a wolf. Romulus killed his brother and founded Rome on the Palatine Hill, beside the Tiber. By the same tradition, seven kings ruled the early city.

steps.title: The kings are driven out
steps.text: Around 509 BC, by tradition, the last king, Tarquin the Proud, was deposed. In place of a monarch the Romans set up a republic of elected magistrates, a senate and assemblies. By 264 BC, when Rome first went to war with Carthage, the city on the Tiber had become a power that looked beyond Italy.

steps.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
steps.text: In 218 BC the Carthaginian general Hannibal left New Carthage in Spain with an army and 37 elephants. He marched through Gaul, crossed the Rhone and went over the Alps by a pass that is still disputed. He reached Italy with about 20,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry, then beat the Romans at the Trebia, at Lake Trasimene and, in 216 BC, at Cannae.

steps.title: Carthage destroyed
steps.text: Hannibal was recalled to defend Africa, and in 202 BC Scipio defeated him at Zama. Half a century later Rome went to war with Carthage a third time. In the spring of 146 BC Scipio Aemilianus stormed the city, destroyed it and sold 50,000 survivors into slavery. In the same year another Roman army sacked and destroyed Corinth in Greece.

steps.title: The Rubicon
steps.text: In January 49 BC Julius Caesar, the conqueror of Gaul, led the Thirteenth Legion across the Rubicon into Italy, where the law forbade a general to bring his army. Suetonius reports that he said the die was cast. Civil war followed and made Caesar dictator for life. He was assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BC.

steps.title: Augustus
steps.text: Caesar's great nephew and heir Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC and took Egypt. In 27 BC the Senate named him Augustus. He kept the outward forms of the Republic and called himself first citizen, but he controlled the armies. He ruled for some forty years, until his death in the year 14.

steps.title: Jerusalem and the Arch of Titus
steps.text: In the year 70 Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian, besieged rebel Jerusalem from April to September and destroyed the Second Temple. The spoils were paraded through Rome in a triumph. Around 81 his brother Domitian raised the Arch of Titus beside the Forum, where a carved relief still shows the Temple's golden menorah.

steps.title: The empire at its height
steps.text: Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest extent. He conquered Dacia, roughly modern Romania, and in 116 organised a province of Mesopotamia. When he died in 117 Rome ruled about five million square kilometres and an estimated 50 to 90 million people. His successor Hadrian withdrew from Mesopotamia and built a wall across Britain.

steps.title: New Rome
steps.text: After half a century of crisis, Diocletian shared rule among four emperors. Constantine, one of their successors, legalised Christianity with the Edict of Milan in 313 and fought his way to sole power by 324. He rebuilt the Greek city of Byzantium as a new capital. It was consecrated on 11 May 330 as New Rome and soon called Constantinople.

steps.title: The sack of Rome
steps.text: When Theodosius I died in 395 the empire was divided between his two sons, one in the east and one in the west. The western court sat at Ravenna when, on 24 August 410, the Visigoths under Alaric entered Rome and plundered it for three days. It was the first time in almost 800 years that the city had fallen to a foreign enemy.

steps.title: The last emperor in the west
steps.text: On 4 September 476 the commander Odoacer took Ravenna and deposed the child emperor Romulus, mocked as Augustulus, the little Augustus. Odoacer sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and pensioned the boy off to an estate near Naples. The date is the usual marker for the end of the Western Roman Empire.

steps.title: Constantinople falls
steps.text: The eastern empire lived on for almost a thousand years more. On 29 May 1453, after a siege of 53 days, the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II broke through the Theodosian Walls with gunpowder artillery. The last emperor, Constantine XI, is said to have died in the fighting. With the city fell the last of a state that had begun with Augustus.
